There is a particular kind of quiet that appears just before rain. The birds negotiate lower branches, leaves turn their pale undersides toward the sky, and even the traffic seems to soften. Nothing has happened yet, but the world is already responding.

I like moments like that—small thresholds where the future becomes briefly visible without becoming certain. A kettle beginning to tremble. A theater dimming. Someone taking a breath before saying what they really mean. They remind us that change rarely arrives all at once. More often, it gathers at the edges.

We tend to celebrate beginnings and endings because they are easy to name. The first day, the final page, the departure, the return. But much of life occurs in the unnamed middle: while skills are still awkward, decisions are still forming, and answers remain incomplete. This can feel frustrating, yet it is where possibility lives. A finished thing can be admired; an unfinished thing can still become almost anything.

Perhaps patience is not simply the ability to wait. Perhaps it is the ability to remain attentive while waiting—to notice the pale leaves, the held breath, the first cool drop on the pavement—and to understand that uncertainty is not empty. It is weather gathering.
